messages.subject: Re: Feature Selection
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hendrik,

First of all, I believed that you already got the email from Mike. For other users, I attach it below.
-------------------

This is Mike Cheng working on the feature selection project. The feature selection was mainly aimed for the data acquired by DIA (data-independent spectral acquisition). The idea is to define a 'gold standard' across-run pattern first, and then select whichever fragments closely following the gold-standard pattern.

In the current MSstats daily, we have a very first version of the feature selection algorithm, where we have the 'Average' (average intensity of each run) as the gold standard pattern. In addition, lambda is a penalized parameter controlling how many fragments should be removed. Simply speaking, if lambda is 0, no fragments would be removed; If lambda is infinity, then every fragments are removed. The bigger the lambda, the more fragments we will penalize (remove). However, we will need to seek an optimal lambda which gives us satisfactorily small estimated prediction error.

Hence, the value of eta is the criterion helping us determine the optimal lambda. Technically speaking, eta is the maximum absolute value of the slope, in the elbow plot where it is predicted residual sum of square versus lambda, we can tolerate as we determine the optimal lambda we want to use. Note that the optimal lambda could vary for each protein. Simply speaking, smaller eta tend to cause a result of removing more fragments.

Suggestions: Using the default values of lambda and eta is recommended unless the outcome is not desirable. We will have better version of the feature selection algorithm ready in MSstats daily. We will define a better 'gold-standard' pattern and control the selection FDR. Furthermore, the users will not need to see and be puzzled by the lambda and eta anymore. This improved version of the feature selection could be available as soon as in a week or two.

----------------------------

and I'm so sorry for my late response. here is about normalization.

Yes, If you had a larger number of proteins in total and also you can assume that large number of proteins among total number of proteins were expected not to change across conditions, then you could normalize across the median intensities of all endogenous signals. (For label-free experiment, you can use 'Normalization='equalizeMedians'.) But, if you have small number of proteins in total, or if you expect that large portion of proteins in total would change across runs or conditions, users should be cautious for 'equalizeMedians' option for label-free experiment and need to use other normalization method, such as considering spike-in standard protein at the experimental design step.

I hope it will be helpful for you. Thank you.

Meena

messages.subject: Re: MSstats normalization
messages.body_plain:
Dear Priyanka,

MSstats decides statistical significance not only based on the fold change, but also based on the associated estimate of variation (called standard error). If a larger fold change has larger associated variation, then it can be an artifact of random chance, and the protein is viewed as not statistically significant. Please take a look at the column 'standard error' in the MSstats output to see the estimates of variation. You can find more details in this paper http://www.biomedcentral.com/1471-2105/13/S16/S6/abstract

I hope this helps
Sincerely
Olga

messages.subject: Re: MSstats normalization
messages.body_plain:
Dear Priyanka,

It is best to generate residual plots on normalized data. Otherwise, deviations from the expected pattern can be due to both a need for normalization and a need for unequal variance.

For large-scale DDA experiments, interference=FALSE, equalFeatureVar=FALSE are good assumptions. They mean that you assume that a protein can have features of varying quality, and that most interferences are noise (i.e. they will not be reproduced if you repeat the experiment).

There is something wrong with the residual plot in the file ProteinX_QuantileUnequalVar.png. If you look at the range of the predicted values (x axis), you see that the values are very small, and are centered around 0. Most likely you normalized the residuals, and tried to re-fit the model to the residuals instead of the log-intensities. I suggest that you quit R to clean all the memory, and repeat the process of normalization, model fitting and residual plots once again.

The time course design means that in your data subjects with identical labels are present in multiple groups. Check your input dataset, and make sure that each replicate has a unique id, regardless of the strain.

I hope this helps
Sincerely
Olga

Hi, I think I am having a similar problem with the latest version of the package. I don't think it is related to the charge, I think it is because of the fragment ion.

I just upgraded to the MSstats.daily version and it seems like this might be a bug (or it is a change in how MSstats behaves). It looks as if it no longer treats the M+1 peak as a separate fragment (I can verify that it didn't treat this as a duplicate in the past). It looks like it only considers the "Feature" column for the purpose of duplicates, which doesn't include fragment information.

For label-free data, should we be summing together the isotopic peaks into a single value, or is it better to treat them as separate fragments? Currently Skyline will output the M+1 peak separately for MSstats output, and previous versions of MSstats allow that as a separate feature. But now it looks like it does not do so.

Also: this is the type of thing that could be reported on GitHub. Is the GitHub repository a good place to report issues?

messages.subject: Re: error group comparison MSstats
messages.body_plain:
Dear Elena,

Sorry for not answering sooner. It seems that you have a problem with the input data format. The error message

'1>CAUTION : the input dataset has incomplete rows'  indicates that some rows in the input data file are missing. MSstats requires that the input file has a separate row for each feature in each run. For example, if a protein has 3 features, 7 disease and 7 control samples, and a labeled reference feature for each endogenous feature, then your input dataset should contain 3 x (7+7) x 2 = 84 rows. If some of the 84 numbers are missing the row should still be present, and the intensity of the missing peak should be denoted as 'NA'. Please check that this is the case for your dataset. For your convenience, the remainder of the error messages lists the names of features for which the number of rows differs from what is expected.

I hope this helps

Olga

Dear James,

Sorry for not answering sooner. Both Meena and I have difficulties interpreting your question. What software do you use to locate and quantify the peaks? Are you talking about quantifying a feature from several peaks in the isotopic distribution? Could you please provide more details, we will do our best to help.

If your question relates to the isotopic distribution, then the important thing is to make the same decision consistently across all the runs. E.g., if a feature is quantified from the most intense peak, then it should be done in every run. Take the sum of intensities of all the peaks in the isotopic distribution is dangerous in presence of missing values.

I  am not sure if I answered your question. Please give us more details, or maybe an example, if this is not the case.

Best wishes
Olga

messages.subject: Re: MS1 Label Free Dataset
messages.body_plain:
We are using Skyline to quantify peaks. Normally, it adds together the peak area from the monoisotopic and M+1 peaks to get a more robust measure of peptide intensity. The "MSstats export" file reports two separate peaks instead. So it outputs e.g.:

PeptideSequence  Charge   FragmentIon     ...   Intensity
SSESKPEFFYSEEQR  2        precursor             2523043
SSESKPEFFYSEEQR  2        precursor [M+1]       3896546

For each peptide in the results. As Skyline was doing this automatically, my interpretation was that this is the desired behavior--that using both peaks separately allowed for a better model. Is this not a good idea?

In any case, the latest version of MSstats rejects this input because the PeptideSequence is the same--even though the FragmentIon column differs, it does not consider them separate features. It looked like Scott Goulding (and maybe Lorenzo Vega) was having the same issue, as I can see that they have multiple isotopic peaks with the same sequence/charge, and MSstats is rejecting them.

Like I said earlier, an older version of MSstats (2.1.3 or 2.2.0, installed via BioConductor) doesn't have an issue with this, so I was wondering if it was a new bug, or an old bug, or a deliberate change in behavior.

thanks for your help,
- James
